messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Hari Patel

Hari Patel was forty-seven when his daughter Priya fell ill. She was nine years old, a bright-eyed girl who loved hiking the trails near their home in the Cascades where Hari worked as a park ranger. One October morning, after a family camping trip, Priya complained of a fever and severe headache. Within hours, her condition deteriorated. The emergency room doctors moved swiftly—spinal tap, antibiotics, the word meningitis spoken in urgent whispers. For three weeks, Hari sat in the pediatric ICU, surrounded by the sharp, chemical smell of antiseptic that seemed to permeate everything—the walls, his clothes, his own skin. He watched his daughter seize, watched her pupils dilate, watched machines beep in rhythms that no parent should have to learn. A resident with alcohol on his breath—Hari could smell it when the man leaned in to examine Priya one evening—had made a medication error that nearly cost her life. Only the quick intervention of a senior physician prevented catastrophe. Priya survived, but those three weeks had fractured something in Hari that no amount of gratitude for her recovery could repair.

In the months that followed, Hari found himself unable to move past what had happened. He replayed the moment he first noticed her fever obsessively, convinced that if he had recognized it sooner, she would never have been admitted. He dwelled on the resident's carelessness—the smell of alcohol on the man's breath became, in Hari's mind, a symbol of negligence, of how easily his daughter's life could have been stolen by someone's inattention. He spent hours in the evenings imagining confrontations, rehearsing what he would say to that resident, what he would do if he ever encountered him again. His wife, Meena, suggested they move forward, that Priya was healthy now, that Hari needed to let it go. But her words only deepened his conviction that she didn't understand the magnitude of what had been taken from them—what could have been taken. He began to dwell on her perceived lack of support during those hospital weeks, her occasional absences to work, her suggestion that they return to normal life. His rumination about her failings, about the resident's negligence, about his own delayed recognition of Priya's symptoms, became a kind of penance, a way of ensuring he would never be caught unprepared again.

This habit of relentless rumination, of turning every moment over in his mind searching for blame and missed warning signs, had begun to reshape his world in ways he didn't fully recognize. Each time he rehearsed a confrontation with the resident or replayed his failure to notice Priya's fever sooner, he was reinforcing the very neural pathways that made innocuous sensations feel dangerous—a hiker's dizziness became not a passing moment but a potential harbinger, the hospital smell not a cleaning product but a signal of imminent catastrophe. His rumination had mapped the world into zones of threat, and now his mind was primed to find danger in places where none existed. When he returned to work as a ranger, leading hikers through the forest trails he loved, he found himself hypervigilant in new ways. A tourist's dizziness on a steep trail sent him spiraling—his own head would swim, his vision would narrow, and suddenly he was back in the ICU watching his daughter's body betray her. The smell of a hiker's hand sanitizer would trigger the same chemical-sharp memory of the hospital. Even the lingering scent of someone's evening drink at a trailhead lodge could send him into a state of agitation that lasted hours. These sensations seemed to come from nowhere, but they were not random—they were the direct consequence of months spent dwelling on danger, on negligence, on the fragility of life. His mind, primed by endless rumination about what could go wrong, had become exquisitely sensitized to any cue that remotely echoed the trauma. A dizziness that a year ago would have been a minor inconvenience now felt like a harbinger. The hospital smell no longer meant cleaning; it meant the moment his world nearly ended. The alcohol smell meant the carelessness that almost took his daughter.

Hari had begun to avoid situations that might trigger these sensations—he volunteered for paperwork instead of leading hikes, he made excuses when colleagues mentioned getting a drink after work, he found reasons not to visit the hospital when Priya needed her follow-up appointments. But each time he stepped back from a trail, each time he declined an invitation, each time he invented a reason not to be present, he was inadvertently expanding the landscape of things that frightened him—the trails themselves became associated with danger, social gatherings with the threat of encountering alcohol and the memories it carried, hospitals with the core trauma itself. His safety behaviors had drawn a map of the event across his entire life, and that map kept growing. When Meena suggested they visit her sister in the city, Hari's chest tightened at the thought of the hospital smell that would inevitably linger in those corridors. He had also come to dread conversations with friends or family who wanted to ask how Priya was doing, because their questions felt like reminders of his failure, of the resident's negligence, of all the ways he had not protected his daughter. His avoidance of these reminders—of people asking about the illness, of places that held the scent of his trauma—had begun to isolate him. But the avoidance itself had become generative: each trail he declined to lead, each hospital visit he postponed, each social gathering he skipped transformed those spaces into repositories of threat. The more he stepped back from the hospital, the more its smell seemed to linger in his imagination—no longer just a chemical scent but a harbinger. The trails he once loved had become, through months of avoidance, the very places his mind now flagged as dangerous, even when he stood nowhere near them. His wife felt the distance growing between them. His colleagues noticed he had become withdrawn, unreliable on the job. The very strategies that had felt necessary to protect himself, to keep his mind vigilant against future disaster, had instead become the bars of a cage he was building around his own life.

Now, after nearly two years of this, Hari has finally agreed to seek help. He is afraid that if he stops dwelling on what happened, if he stops being vigilant, he will miss the next warning sign. But he is also afraid—though he speaks of this more quietly—that he is losing his family, that Priya, now recovering beautifully, is beginning to notice her father's fear whenever he looks at her.

violation_explanations: The vignette describes maladaptive strategies (avoidance, safety behaviors, rumination) and triggers (sensations, smells, situations), but does not establish a causal relationship where these strategies drive or create new triggers; instead, the narrative shows triggers activating avoidance, and avoidance reinforcing threat associations, but not the reverse causal direction required by the edge.
